newsitem.title: UK: De Beers puts pressure on Russia on diamond deal.
newsitem.headline: De Beers puts pressure on Russia on diamond deal.

text.p: South African diamond mining giant De Beers on Wednesday turned the screw on Russia to approve a new diamond trade pact, threatening to stop doing business next year under the terms of an interim deal.

"What we are saying is that we expect to be talking to the Russians about buying from them again in 1997 but we are not prepared to go on on precisely the same basis," Tim Capon, director of De Beers' Central Selling Organisation (CSO), told Reuters.

De Beers, which also announced record diamond sales for 1996, wants to review its relationship with the Russian authorities in 1997 as Russia still has not given the green light to a new sales agreement, Capon said.
The CSO markets about 75 percent of all the world's rough diamond production with Russia making up about 20 percent of total CSO sales.
De Beers has been in protracted talks with Russia to reach a new sales agreement after a five-year deal officially expired at the end of last year.
That pact, however, has remained operational as long as no new one was agreed.
Approval has been delayed by political bickering in Russia, where different ministries and factions in the diamond industry battle for control over diamond cash flows.
A breakthrough for a new agreement seemed close when De Beers signed a memorandum of understanding with the Russian government in February.

All that was needed then was a final agreement with Almazy Rossii-Sakha (ARS), Russia's major diamond producer. A deal was reached in September, with both parties waiting since then for approval from the Russian government.
De Beers, meanwhile, continued buying rough diamonds under the old agreement.

"These arrangements have not operated satisfactorily in 1996 and therefore De Beers has indicated to the Russian government and ARS that it is not prepared to continue to buy diamonds under the old agreement beyond December 31, 1996," De Beers said.
It said it still hoped a new deal will be approved in due course.

De Beers also announced that the CSO's rough diamond sales rose seven percent to $4.834 billion in 1996 from $4.531 billion in 1995, reflecting continuing strength in world retail demand for diamond jewellery, particularly in the American market.
It said that retail sales of diamond jewellery in 1995, the latest figures available, rose on average by an estimated five percent to a record level, with the U.S. market increasing by eight percent.
De Beers said that in Europe, 1995 sales remained mixed, with Britain, France and Italy performing well.
Taiwan remained a weak spot in east Asia, where there was generally continued strong growth. Sales in Japan showed signs of a recovery in a difficult economic environment, De Beers added.
